1.q: יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ בֶּן חִלְקִיָּ֑הוּ מִן הַ⁠כֹּֽהֲנִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּ⁠עֲנָת֔וֹת בְּ⁠אֶ֖רֶץ בִּנְיָמִֽן
1.note: Here the author is introducing **Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a certain man named Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, who was one of the priests living in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin]

The implication is that Jeremiah himself belonged to one of the priestly families that lived in Anathoth. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who was one of the priests living in Anathoth]
The word **Anathoth** is the name of a town.

2.note: The author is using **which was the word of Yahweh to him** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to whom Yahweh gave messages.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to whom Yahweh spoke his messages]

2.q: בִּ⁠ימֵ֛י יֹאשִׁיָּ֥הוּ בֶן אָמ֖וֹן מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה
2.note: Here, **the days of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah** represents the time when Josiah, son of Amon, was ruling as king over Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [during the time when Josiah, son of Amon, was reigning as king over Judah]
The word **Amon** is the name of a man.

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **thirteenth**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year 13 of his reign]

3.note: Here, **Jerusalem** represents the people who lived in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [until the exile of the people of Jerusalem]

The **fifth** month of the Hebrew calendar includes parts of July and August on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

4.note: Jeremiah is using the phrase translated as **And the word of Yahweh was to me** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

In the previous verses, the author referred to Jeremiah in the third person, saying that the word of Yahweh came “to him.” Beginning here, Jeremiah speaks of himself in the first person, saying that the word of Yahweh was **to me**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this shift clear to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the word of Yahweh was to me, Jeremiah]

5.q: בְּ⁠טֶ֨רֶם אצור⁠ך בַ⁠בֶּ֨טֶן֙ יְדַעְתִּ֔י⁠ךָ וּ⁠בְ⁠טֶ֛רֶם תֵּצֵ֥א מֵ⁠רֶ֖חֶם הִקְדַּשְׁתִּ֑י⁠ךָ
5.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Even before you were born, I truly knew you and set you apart for myself]

The implication is that the **belly** in view is the womb of Jeremiah’s mother. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in your mother’s belly, I knew]

The implication is that when Yahweh says that he **knew** Jeremiah, he means that he had already chosen him for a special purpose. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the belly, I had already selected you for my purposes]

Yahweh is using **before you came out from the womb** as a common expression of the culture to mean “before you were born.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and before your birth]

The implication is that the messages Jeremiah would speak as **a prophet** would concern **the nations**, not the people of Judah only. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I appointed you a prophet whose messages would be for the nations]

6.note: Jeremiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of dismay. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh no, Lord Yahweh]

Jeremiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

The implication is that Jeremiah does not have the skill to speak publicly the way a prophet would need to speak. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I do not know how to speak persuasively in public]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because I am a youth]

7.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Do not say that you are a youth]

7.q: עַֽל כָּל אֲשֶׁ֤ר אֶֽשְׁלָחֲ⁠ךָ֙ תֵּלֵ֔ךְ וְ⁠אֵ֛ת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲצַוְּ⁠ךָ֖ תְּדַבֵּֽר
7.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about where Jeremiah would go and what he would say after the verbs rather than before them. Alternate translation: [you shall go to all to whom I shall send you, and you shall speak all that I command you]

8.note: Here, **their faces** represents the people themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Do not be afraid of them]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **afraid**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [Be brave in front of them]

The pronoun **their** refers to the people to whom Yahweh will send Jeremiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [of the faces of the people to whom I send you]

Jeremiah is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

9.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֤ח יְהוָה֙ אֶת יָד֔⁠וֹ וַ⁠יַּגַּ֖ע עַל פִּ֑⁠י
9.note: Reaching out and touching Jeremiah’s mouth was a symbolic action by which Yahweh showed that he was giving Jeremiah the very words that he would speak as a prophet. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Then Yahweh stretched out his hand and touched my mouth to show that he was giving me his words to speak]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the messages he would give Jeremiah were objects that he could place **in your mouth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have given you my messages to speak]

10.q: רְאֵ֞ה הִפְקַדְתִּ֣י⁠ךָ הַ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֗ה עַל הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֙ וְ⁠עַל הַ⁠מַּמְלָכ֔וֹת לִ⁠נְת֥וֹשׁ וְ⁠לִ⁠נְת֖וֹץ וּ⁠לְ⁠הַאֲבִ֣יד וְ⁠לַ⁠הֲר֑וֹס לִ⁠בְנ֖וֹת וְ⁠לִ⁠נְטֽוֹעַ
10.note: Here, the word **to** at the beginning of the phrase **to pluck up and to pull down and to destroy and to throw down, to build and to plant** marks that phrase as the goal or purpose of **I am appointing you this day over the nations and over the kingdoms**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

10.q: הִפְקַדְתִּ֣י⁠ךָ הַ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֗ה עַל הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֙ וְ⁠עַל הַ⁠מַּמְלָכ֔וֹת
10.note: The implication is that Jeremiah would exercise this authority **over the nations and over the kingdoms** by speaking the messages that Yahweh gave him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I am appointing you this day to speak with my authority over the nations and over the kingdoms]

10.q: לִ⁠נְת֥וֹשׁ וְ⁠לִ⁠נְת֖וֹץ וּ⁠לְ⁠הַאֲבִ֣יד וְ⁠לַ⁠הֲר֑וֹס לִ⁠בְנ֖וֹת וְ⁠לִ⁠נְטֽוֹעַ
10.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of what he will accomplish through the messages Jeremiah speaks as if Jeremiah were a farmer who would **pluck up** and **plant** crops and a builder who would **pull down** and **build**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to remove and to demolish and to ruin and to overthrow, and to establish and to cause to flourish]

The terms **to pluck up**, **to pull down**, **to destroy**, and **to throw down** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the four terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to completely demolish]

11.note: An **almond** is a kind of nut that grows on a tree. It was common in this part of the world. If your readers would not be familiar with what an almond is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a branch from a nut tree]

12.note: Yahweh is using **You have seen well** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you have seen correctly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have seen correctly]

12.q: כִּֽי שֹׁקֵ֥ד אֲנִ֛י עַל דְּבָרִ֖⁠י לַ⁠עֲשֹׂתֽ⁠וֹ
12.note: Yahweh is using a wordplay here. In the original language, the word for “almond” in the previous verse sounds almost the same as the word translated as **watching** in this verse. If your language has a way to indicate this kind of wordplay, you could use it here, or you could explain the wordplay in a footnote.

13.note: The expression **blown-on** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a pot that someone is blowing on to heat it]

The implication is that someone has been fanning a fire underneath the pot, so that what is inside it is boiling. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a pot boiling over a fanned fire]

Jeremiah is using **its face {is away} from the face of the north** as a common expression of the culture. This could mean: (1) the pot was tipping away from the north, so that its boiling contents would spill out toward Judah or (2) the pot was facing away from the north. If this phrase does not have a clear meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it is tilting away from the north]

14.note: The implication is that **the north** is the direction from which invading armies would come into the land of Judah. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [From the north, where invading armies come from, disaster will be released]

The expression **will be released** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will unleash disaster]

The implication is that **the land** here is the land of Judah. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the inhabitants of the land of Judah]

15.q: כִּ֣י הִנְ⁠נִ֣י קֹרֵ֗א לְ⁠כָֽל מִשְׁפְּח֛וֹת מַמְלְכ֥וֹת צָפ֖וֹנָ⁠ה
15.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because I am calling to all the clans of the kingdoms of the north]

Yahweh is using **behold me calling** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am about to summon these armies.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to call]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the clans** that make up **the kingdoms of the north**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to all the clans that make up the kingdoms in the north]
Jeremiah is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. See how you translated this expression in 1:8.

15.q: וְֽ⁠נָתְנוּ֩ אִ֨ישׁ כִּסְא֜⁠וֹ פֶּ֣תַח שַׁעֲרֵ֣י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֗ם
15.note: Setting up a throne at the entrance of a city’s gates was a symbolic action by which a conquering king showed that he now ruled that city. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and each man will claim rule by setting his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem]

16.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I have decided]

The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Judah, not to the invaders whom Yahweh has just described. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [against the people of Judah concerning all their evil]

The implication is that **what they made with their own hands** were idols. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the idols that they themselves crafted]

17.q: וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ תֶּאְזֹ֣ר מָתְנֶ֔י⁠ךָ וְ⁠קַמְתָּ֙ וְ⁠דִבַּרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם אֵ֛ת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י אֲצַוֶּ֑⁠ךָּ
17.note: The pronouns **you yourself** and **I myself** are emphatic in the original language. Yahweh uses them to contrast what Jeremiah must do with what Yahweh himself will do. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [So as for you, gird your loins and stand up and say to them all that I, for my part, shall command you]

Here Yahweh is speaking of getting ready for hard work as if it were tucking one’s long robe into one’s belt, which is what the expression **gird your loins** describes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you yourself shall get ready for hard work]

17.q: אַל תֵּחַת֙ מִ⁠פְּנֵי⁠הֶ֔ם פֶּֽן אֲחִתְּ⁠ךָ֖ לִ⁠פְנֵי⁠הֶֽם
17.note: Here, **lest** marks **I dismay you before their faces** as the negative goal or purpose of **Do not be dismayed from before their faces**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **dismay**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [Have courage]

Here, **before their faces** represents in their presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [lest I dismay you in their presence]

The expression **be dismayed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Do not let them dismay you]

18.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I have made** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is the one who has made Jeremiah strong and secure. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself have made you]

Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus Jeremiah’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

18.q: נְתַתִּ֣י⁠ךָ הַ⁠יּ֗וֹם לְ⁠עִ֨יר מִבְצָ֜ר וּ⁠לְ⁠עַמּ֥וּד בַּרְזֶ֛ל וּ⁠לְ⁠חֹמ֥וֹת נְחֹ֖שֶׁת
18.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of Jeremiah as if he were **a city of fortification and an iron pillar and bronze walls**, that is, things that enemies would not be able to break through. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have made you this day someone whom no one will be able to overcome]
Yahweh is speaking of something that he will certainly do as if he had already done it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the future tense here.

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **city** that is characterized by **fortification**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a fortified city]

Here, **the land** represents the people who live in the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [against all the people who live in the land]

19.note: Yahweh uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between the people fighting against Jeremiah and their failure to overcome him. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, they will not prevail]
